subtype: Approach: asks what a good enough choice would be and what reversing it would cost [Revision]
passage:
Okay, so I'm Afreen, and this was about picking a club in my first month of college. There were four I liked: dance, debating, the coding group and the film club. I spent a whole week on a table of hours, meeting days and who ran what.
Then, at midnight, staring at the table, I asked myself something I hadn't asked before. What would it actually cost to undo this? And the answer was a few Saturdays. That's all. Clubs let you leave.
So the question changed. Not which is perfect, but which one is good enough to try. I chose the film club, went to the first meeting, and liked it. The evenings I'd been losing on that table went to the maths course I actually needed.

qa.q: How many clubs did Afreen like at the start?
qa.a: Afreen liked four: dance, debating, the coding group and the film club.

qa.q: What did Afreen feel once the cost of a wrong choice became clear?
qa.a: Afreen felt relieved and lighter, because undoing the choice would only cost a few Saturdays.

qa.q: What else could Afreen do if the film club turned out to be a poor fit?
qa.a: Afreen could leave and try the debating group, since the choice is easy to reverse and a month of trying tells more than a table does.

qa.q: How might the maths course look to Afreen's college schedule now, compared with before?
qa.a: With the table given up, the evenings are free for the maths course Afreen needed, so the quick decision made room for the more important task.

grounding: A student asks what a good enough club choice would be and what reversing it would cost, then decides and moves on.

subtype: Approach: asks what a good enough choice would be and what reversing it would cost [Revision]
passage: I'm Hafsa, and Divyansh and I were in the same first-year batch. For a whole week he agonised over the sports elective: badminton, swimming or yoga. He made lists. He asked seniors. He went to see the pool twice. On Thursday evening I found him outside the sports office staring at the notice board. Then I watched his face change. He tapped a line on the notice and read it out: "Students may switch electives in the first two weeks." He laughed at himself. "So if I hate it, I just switch. Why am I treating this like marriage?" He wrote "badminton" on the form in about ten seconds and handed it in. That night he was back in the library, working on the coding assignment he'd been putting off.

qa.q: What did the line on the notice board say?
qa.a: "Students may switch electives in the first two weeks."

qa.q: What might Divyansh have felt when he laughed at himself?
qa.a: He seemed relieved and a bit embarrassed at how much worry he'd put into a choice he could undo.

qa.q: What else could Divyansh ask himself before future choices?
qa.a: Whether the choice can be reversed and what that would cost; if it's cheap to undo, choose a good-enough option quickly.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see the change in Divyansh?
qa.a: Hafsa seems amused and glad to see him drop the agonising and get back to the assignment.

grounding: Realising the choice can be changed later, a student picks a reasonable option and spends the time saved on something more important.

passage:
Monday: Arnab had to pick a foreign language for his second year: German, French or Japanese. He opened eleven tabs of comparisons and asked Gautam, his roommate, for the third time which had "better scope".

Wednesday: Still undecided, he found the course handbook in his inbox. Gautam pointed at page four: "Language can be changed at the end of the first term with no penalty." Arnab sat back. "So the worst case is I lose one term of French and switch." He picked French because the class timing fit his lab schedule, closed the tabs and sent the form.

The next Monday: Arnab spent the evening he'd have used for comparing on his circuits project, which was due first.

qa.q: When can the language be changed, according to the handbook?
qa.a: At the end of the first term with no penalty.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel once he saw page four?
qa.a: He felt relieved and lighter, realising the worst case was small and the choice didn't have to be perfect.

qa.q: Which choice helped Arnab most, and why?
qa.a: Asking what reversing the choice would cost; once it was low, a good-enough option was enough.

qa.q: How might Gautam see Arnab's decision?
qa.a: Gautam is probably relieved not to be asked about "scope" a fourth time.

grounding: A student realises a choice can be reversed, picks a reasonable option and uses the saved time on work that matters more.
